To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. ## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it; Python is available as `python3`. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

E7 looks like a shared liberty between White's two groups, so playing there would reduce both to 2 libs each, but my E7 stone itself would only have 2 liberties (D7, E8), leaving it vulnerable to a White atari at D7.

Tracing it further, if White plays E8 instead, it puts my E7 stone into atari, and extending to D7 doesn't fully solve it since White can keep chasing with D6 or D8 — this line looks too thin and probably loses the stone. Trying D6 instead: it cuts the D5 group down to 2 liberties, but White can respond with E7 to connect both groups, undermining the attack.

Checking C5 as another approach: it also leaves White with escape moves via B5 or C6, since C5 only has 2 liberties itself. I'm also considering whether White's D5-E5-E6 group is actually connected to C4 — it isn't yet, so White needs a connecting move like C5 or D6, which a 14k opponent might miss.

Going back to the E7-E8 exchange, after White plays E8 putting me in atari, I could try E9 to look for a capturing race against the E8-F7-F8-F9-G9 group, checking its remaining liberties at D8 and E9.

This race looks messy and risky — both E7 and E9 would be in atari with only one liberty each, and White has multiple ways to extend or capture. Given the opponent's weaker level, I think it's safer to avoid this complicated fight and instead look at solid moves like H8 to shore up the H9 group, or G6 to firmly connect my F5-F6 and G7-G8 groups, since a White cut at G6 would quickly run out of liberties and get captured anyway.

I'm also considering D6 as a probing cut to weaken the D5 and C7 groups, but White's natural response at E7 would merge those groups into one with plenty of liberties, leaving my D6 stone thin with only two liberties. Given I'm already ahead by roughly four points on my rough count, it feels wiser to play calmly for secure endgame points rather than force a complicated fight.

Checking A3 hane doesn't work well since it isn't connected to anything useful. H8 seems like a small safe move to secure H9, though I'm also considering an attacking move around E7 instead.

Actually E7 is the key point since white's D5 and F7 groups both only have three liberties and share that connection point. If I take E7 I need to read out whether it survives: white likely responds E8, I play D7, then white tries D6 to connect into the D5 group and atari my stones, forcing me to extend to D8 to keep liberties alive.

That D8 extension simultaneously drops the F-group's liberties down to just E9, so it's a double-edged fight — white's best try looks like D9, which both ataris my chain and tries to defend the F-group's liberty, but I need to check whether D9 actually connects to E8 or leaves E9 as a capturable point for me.

Confirming F-group has only E9 as a liberty, so playing there nets me five stones cleanly. The deeper risk is that a weaker engine might misplay this, but since the fight happens entirely inside white's area under area scoring, even the worst case of losing my E7/D7 stones costs nothing extra beyond a tempo — and with my 4-point lead, that's a cheap gamble for a potentially huge gain, as long as my F5-F6 group stays safe. I also want to check the other atari line where white tries D7 against E7 and I respond with E8.

Tracing it out, after I play E8 my E7-E8 group only has D8 and E9 as liberties while white's F-group is down to just E9 — if white tries to save it by playing E9, their liberties shrink to just D9 and I can capture six stones with D9. Alternatively if white tries D8 to atari me first, I still escape by taking E9 and capturing the F-group. Either way E7 holds up as a strong move, so I'll play it.
